paper.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
paper.central_claim: LM pipelines can be written as declarative parameterised modules and automatically optimised (compiled) by teleprompters, producing self-improving pipelines that outperform standard few-shot prompting and rival expert-written prompt chains.

provenance.notes: actual_model/session_id/receipt_ref not exposed to the worker; null by design (no probing).

rationale: Metric-filtered trace bootstrapping and demo search with clean train/dev/test splits; test parity with expert demos is 0.5 pp, compile effect confounded with dev search and ensembles, no variance or cost accounting. Retained level, scoped.

missing_sections: exact GPT-3.5 and Llama2 checkpoints, sampling temperatures and per-run variance are not given in the paper

evidence.quote: Unfortunately, existing LM pipelines are typically implemented using hard-coded
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap: hand-written prompt templates in LM pipelines.

evidence.quote: We argue that this approach, while pervasive, can be brittle and unscalable
evidence.support_explanation: Claim of brittleness; supported by informal codebase census (E023), not by experiment.

evidence.quote: Within minutes of compiling, a few lines of DSPy allow GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat to self-bootstrap pipelines that outperform standard few-shot prompting
evidence.support_explanation: Central empirical claim.

evidence.quote: The program’s metric is used to filter for multi-stage traces that together help the pipeline pass the metric.
evidence.support_explanation: Selection rule for bootstrapped demonstrations: end-to-end metric on final output only.

evidence.quote: not the intermediate steps
evidence.support_explanation: Only final-output labels are assumed; intermediate demonstrations are bootstrapped from the LM itself.

evidence.quote: Many hyperparameter tuning algorithms (e.g., random search or Tree-structured Parzen Estimators as in HyperOpt (Bergstra et al., 2013) and Optuna (Akiba et al., 2019)) can be applied for selection among candidates.
evidence.support_explanation: Candidate selection reuses off-the-shelf search over demonstration sets.

evidence.quote: In this iteration of DSPy, we focus on demonstrations and find that simple rejection-sampling-like approaches can help bootstrap highly effective multi-stage systems.
evidence.support_explanation: Operation: rejection sampling of traces; instruction optimisation is not the evaluated mechanism.

evidence.quote: We focus primarily on automatically generating and selecting useful demonstrations.
evidence.support_explanation: Optimised parameter is the demonstration set.

evidence.quote: We sample 200 and 300 question–answer pairs from the official training set for training and development, respectively. Our final evaluations use the 1.3k official test set examples.
evidence.support_explanation: GSM8K split: 200 train, 300 dev from official train; 1.3k official test.

evidence.quote: We report extensive comparisons on the development set to avoid overfitting on test.
evidence.support_explanation: Dev set drives comparisons and candidate selection; test reported for representatives only.

evidence.quote: We report the average of 3–5 runs (depending on the setting) when applying such random sampling.
evidence.support_explanation: Only the random-sampling LabeledFewShot baseline is averaged over runs; no variance for compiled programs.

evidence.quote: fewshot + human_CoT 78.6 72.4 34.3 33.7 bootstrap trainset 80.3 72.9 43.3 – + ensemble trainset 88.3 81.6 43.7 –
evidence.support_explanation: GPT-3.5 CoT: bootstrap 72.9 test vs expert human CoT demos 72.4 (0.5 pp); ensemble 81.6 is a 7-program vote compared with unensembled expert baseline.

evidence.quote: An ensemble will bootstrap multiple copies of the same program, and then replace the program with a new one that runs them all in parallel and reduces their predictions into one with a custom function (e.g., majority voting).
evidence.support_explanation: Ensembling multiplies inference cost.

evidence.quote: A program that ensembles the top-7 candidate programs from a bootstrapping compiler run
evidence.support_explanation: Seven programs are voted in the ensemble rows.

evidence.quote: compiling generally runs on the order of minutes (or tens of minutes) as even the more expensive settings only require running the program a few thousand times (e.g., 10–20 trials over 150–300 validation examples)
evidence.support_explanation: Compile cost given qualitatively; no tokens or dollars; baselines not charged.

evidence.quote: the prompt allows the LM to leverage the answer field for reasoning first, which is permitted as the metric extracts the final numerical value for evaluation
evidence.support_explanation: The vanilla program learns to reason inside the answer field; a program-structure effect, not only demonstration quality.

evidence.quote: Compiling the correct modules, instead of string prompts, improves different LMs from 4–20% accuracy to 49–88% accuracy
evidence.support_explanation: Headline compares unoptimised vanilla programs with compiled CoT/reflection programs, mixing program structure and compilation.

evidence.quote: The HotPotQA test set is hidden, so we reserve the official validation set for our testing, and sample 1000 examples for that.
evidence.support_explanation: HotPotQA test is the official validation set subset.

evidence.quote: The marked result is evaluated on 50% of our test set due to cost.
evidence.support_explanation: The ensemble test result uses half the test set.

evidence.quote: we leave reporting on such tasks under controlled experimental conditions to future work
evidence.support_explanation: Other tasks are anecdotal; evidence is two benchmarks.

evidence.quote: they note that GPT-4 was in fact pre-trained on a subset of GSM8K
evidence.support_explanation: Authors flag contamination for GPT-4 but not for GPT-3.5 or Llama2 used in their experiments.

evidence.quote: Researchers are starting to apply discrete optimization and RL to find effective prompts, generally for a single logical LM call
evidence.support_explanation: Nearest optimisation neighbours (APE-style, RL, LM-feedback prompt optimisers) are described in one sentence; no head-to-head comparison.

evidence.quote: In late September 2023, we found that the LangChain codebase contains 50 strings exceeding 1000 characters
evidence.support_explanation: Informal evidence for the hand-prompt gap.

evidence.quote: generalize the ideas on zero-shot prompting and rationale self-generation from Kojima et al. (2022), Zelikman et al. (2022)
evidence.support_explanation: STaR-style rationale bootstrapping is the closest ancestor of demonstration bootstrapping; it appears only in a footnote.

evidence.quote: This program scores 39.3% answer EM and 46.0% passage accuracy on the dev set, using only 200 labeled inputs and 800 unlabeled questions.
evidence.support_explanation: BootstrapFinetune to T5-Large (weights; outside harness-only scope, reported on dev).

evidence.quote: H2 Parameterizing the modules and treating prompting as an optimization problem makes DSPy better at adapting to different LMs, and it may outperform expert-written prompts.
evidence.support_explanation: Stated hypothesis tested by the case studies.
Counterexample: single bootstrap is below expert human reasoning demonstrations for ReAct on dev (31.0 vs 33.0; 24.7 vs 28.3); bootstrap x2 recovers.

evidence.quote: we can match or surpass this using bootstrap, substantiating our hypothesis that DSPy can cut the need for hand-crafted prompts
evidence.support_explanation: Reading of the human-CoT comparison; test difference is 0.5 pp for GPT-3.5 and Llama2 test cell is missing.

signatures.object: Demonstrations (and optionally weights) of each Predict module in a multi-stage LM pipeline; baseline: hand-written prompt templates / random labeled few-shot
signatures.information: Training inputs with at most final-output labels; metric function; teacher or zero-shot program; traces of every module call
signatures.operation: Run teacher program on training inputs, keep traces whose final output passes the metric, store them as per-module demonstrations; optionally random search / Optuna over demo subsets using a dev set; optionally nest or ensemble
signatures.output: Compiled program (Python object holding demos) ; optionally finetuned small LM
signatures.conditions: Metric computable on final output; program decomposed so that some training inputs yield passing traces
signatures.selection_rule/data: Metric filter on training traces; best of random-search trials on dev (16 trials in pseudocode); top-7 for ensembles
signatures.persistence: Demonstrations stored in the compiled program
signatures.later_use: Injected in the prompt of each module for all later inputs
signatures.claimed_effect: GSM8K and HotPotQA accuracy gains (e.g. GPT-3.5 CoT 72.9 test, ensemble 81.6; multihop test 39.6 EM, ensemble 45.6 on half set)
signatures.failure_boundary: No regression/rollback rule; no handling of metric gaming; compile needs a program that can already pass the metric on some inputs

signatures.object: Pipeline program expressed as signatures and modules
signatures.operation: Replace string prompts with signature-defined modules (Predict, ChainOfThought, ReAct, MultiChainComparison)
signatures.claimed_effect: H1: comparable quality without hand-crafted prompts
signatures.failure_boundary: program structure effect confounded with compilation (E016, E017)

gap.author_gap: LM pipelines depend on long hand-written prompt templates that are brittle and unscalable across LMs, tasks and pipelines.
gap.checked_gap: Real and widely recognised; supported by an informal LangChain census and by the dependence of results on demonstrations in Table 1. Closest optimisation neighbours (single-call prompt optimisers, STaR-style rationale bootstrapping, Reflexion) are named in one sentence or a footnote and not compared experimentally.
gap.lineage/closest_adjacent: DSP (own predecessor), CoT/ReAct prompting, STaR-style rationale bootstrapping, discrete/RL prompt optimisers for single calls, LangChain/LlamaIndex prompt libraries.
gap.residue: No unified way to optimise multi-stage pipelines without intermediate labels.
gap.stakes: Manual prompt engineering cost and brittleness across LMs.
gap.method_response: Declarative modules plus teleprompters that bootstrap per-module demonstrations from metric-filtered traces and select among candidates.
gap.remaining_gap: Optimiser generality beyond demonstrations; comparison with other optimisers; guarantee against metric gaming; variance.
gap.unresolved: Contemporaneous prompt optimisers and STaR were not read in full here; the novelty of multi-stage trace bootstrapping relative to them is author-asserted.

matches.tactic_steps_checked: Manufacture per-module supervision (demonstrations) from the model own traces filtered by the end-to-end metric: executed. C08 requires a generator reaching beyond corpus support and a single quality gate with iterated retraining; DSPy has the gate (metric) and optional nesting but generates in-distribution demonstrations on the same training inputs, so sub is left null. C07 (internal state) and C26 (objective-level preference) fit worse.
matches.success_failure_checks: Oral-style conditions: explicit filter stage (met, but its removal is not ablated); intervention-based causal validation (unmet); simple fine-tune baseline (unmet). Failure modes: thin wrapper on existing machinery (partial), missing isolating baselines (partial).
matches.reason: Bootstrapped demonstrations are model-generated, metric-filtered supervision for intermediate steps that have no labels.

matches.tactic_steps_checked: Prompting is recast as hyper-parameter optimisation over demonstration candidates solved with random search / TPE; the reduction is asserted, not proven.
matches.success_failure_checks: RE-3 new identifying structure: the new part is multi-stage trace credit, search machinery is existing.
matches.reason: A different operation (optimisation framing) from signal manufacture.

rs_pattern.reason: Both matches partial, no sub-card fits.
rs_pattern.resolves_problem_reason: Compiled programs match or beat the tested hand-crafted baselines on two benchmarks, but the gap that hand-crafted prompts are brittle is not closed beyond those cases and optimiser budget/variance are uncontrolled (E012, E015, E020).

matches.condition_checks: H13 steps: (1) genome = demonstration set, edit operator = metric-filtered bootstrap and random subset, no LLM mutation (partial); (2) fitness defined before search: end-to-end metric credited across pipeline modules, S1 met; (3) scoring/reporting separation: train/dev/test stated (met); (4) explicit budget and optimiser cost: only qualitative (unmet); (5) ablate against simpler selector and no-search baseline: fewshot random baseline exists, but not a same-trial random-search baseline (partial). F2/F3 not triggered.

unassigned: Programming-abstraction contribution (signatures/modules) is a framework contribution with no domain card; weight-finetune teleprompter (BootstrapFinetune) is outside the harness scope (A3).
revision_proposals: population_search_executable_fitness H13: add note that demonstration-set bootstrapping by rejection sampling (no LLM mutation) is an in-scope variant, to be decided at stage end (not applied).

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: RS: derive a training signal from the model own outputs and filter it; RSI H13: candidate prompt text (here demonstrations) scored by executable metric and selected. Both rely on metric-filtered self-generated text.
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions_differences: H13 expects LLM-driven variation and budgeted allocation; DSPy uses rejection sampling and random subsets with unstated allocation. RS C08-style retraining loop only appears as optional nesting.

claims.text: Compiled DSPy programs outperform standard few-shot prompting generally by over 25% (GPT-3.5) and 65% (llama2-13b-chat) within minutes.
claims.baseline/control: none, random labeled fewshot (avg of 3-5 sampling runs), human CoT demos
claims.selection_vs_test: dev for comparison and search, test for representative rows
claims.result/denominator: e.g. GPT-3.5 vanilla 25.2 -> 61.7 test; CoT 72.4 human vs 72.9 bootstrap; multihop 31.2 -> 39.6 EM
claims.allowed_conclusion: On these two tasks and LMs, compiling raised held-out accuracy over zero-shot and random few-shot; part of the headline gain comes from program structure (CoT/reflection/multihop).

claims.text: Bootstrapped demonstrations match or surpass expert-written demonstrations.
claims.result/denominator: GSM8K GPT-3.5 test 72.9 vs 72.4; Llama2 test cell missing; ReAct dev 31.0 vs 33.0 (single bootstrap)
claims.allowed_conclusion: Parity at best in some cells; superiority only with extra stages (bootstrap x2, ensemble).

claims.text: Small LMs compiled by DSPy are competitive with expert-prompted proprietary pipelines.
claims.result/denominator: T5-Large 39.3 EM dev; literature figures on different samples
claims.allowed_conclusion: Informal; T5 weight-finetune result outside harness scope.

assessment.evidence_level_reason: Compiled demonstrations (a retained non-weight change selected on train/dev) improve accuracy on a separate official test set; no improver comparison is made.
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: Bootstrapping metric-filtered traces into per-module demonstrations raised held-out accuracy of simple pipelines on GSM8K and HotPotQA for GPT-3.5 and Llama2-13b-chat above zero-shot and random few-shot baselines, reaching parity with expert demonstrations in some cells (author-reported).
assessment.unresolved: Variance, same-budget baselines, filter ablation, comparison with other prompt optimisers, contamination, exact LM versions.

retention_trace.proposed_change: bootstrapped per-module demonstrations (and optional finetuned small LM)
retention_trace.selection: metric filter on training traces; dev-set random search; top-7 ensemble
retention_trace.measured_gain: test accuracy gains on GSM8K and HotPotQA (author-reported)

G.reason: Concrete, widely recognised bottleneck (hand-written prompts in multi-stage pipelines) with an informal census and clear lineage to DSP and library practice; the nearest optimisation and rationale-bootstrapping neighbours are cited in one sentence/footnote only.

M.reason: The mechanism (final-metric rejection sampling gives per-module labels, candidate selection by search) is clear, its assumptions are stated (decomposable programs, a metric) and predictions differ from random few-shot; scope is demonstrations only and novelty over STaR-style bootstrapping is weakly argued.

X.reason: Compiler stages, pseudocode, parameters (k=8, 16 trials, top-7), data splits and example programs allow reconstruction; no regression/rollback or metric-gaming handling, and LM versions/temperatures are not given.

E.measurement.reason: Final numeric accuracy and answer EM are objective and applied on held-out sets with none/few-shot baselines; the vanilla program learns reasoning inside the answer field and cross-paper comparisons use different samples.

E.causality.reason: Compile vs none vs random few-shot vs human demos is informative, but the compile effect is confounded with dev-set search (up to 16 trials) and 7-way ensembles that baselines do not get, the metric filter is not ablated, and program-structure effects are mixed into the headline.

E.holdout.reason: Train/dev/test are separated and test is official; weaknesses are two benchmarks, test results for selected rows only and unaddressed pretraining contamination for GPT-3.5 and Llama2.

E.statistics.reason: Split sizes are stated, but only the random few-shot baseline is averaged over 3-5 runs; compiled programs have single numbers with no seeds, intervals or tests, and parity claims rest on a 0.5 pp test difference.

E.cost.reason: Compile cost is given only as minutes and a few thousand program runs; no tokens or dollars, ensemble inference multiplies cost, and baselines are not charged for search or voting.
